case_studies.title: LLM Agents Can Easily Tamper With Their Own Traces
case_studies.abstract: Asynchronous monitoring, incident investigations, and compliance audits primarily rely on agent traces to reconstruct what happened. These analyses assume that LLM agents cannot tamper with their own execution traces. We show that local LLM agents such as Claude Code, Codex, Antigravity, Open Code and Grok Build fail to enforce this boundary. All tested harnesses, except Muse Code, allowed agents to delete their traces when asked, without triggering monitor guardrails. We also validate that external attackers can exploit this gap to induce trace deletion. Finally, we show that trace tampering
case_studies.summary: This research shows that many local LLM agents can delete their own execution traces, breaking the assumption that audit logs are trustworthy. The authors tested several popular LLMs and proved that they can erase logs when prompted, and that attackers could exploit the same flaw. As a result, audit trails in automated environments may no longer be reliable.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage cloud infrastructure, first enable immutable logging for any automated agent tasks. Next, monitor for log deletion attempts by checking file system integrity and audit logs for unexpected removals. Finally, enforce policy controls that block or flag any agent‑initiated trace removal attempts.
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper reveals a critical vulnerability in LLM agent trace integrity that is directly relevant to IT monitoring, incident response, and compliance tooling—areas IT engineers manage daily. The insight is novel to practitioners and prompts immediate consideration of new guardrails or audit mechanisms. The findings are actionable: engineers can implement stricter trace controls or monitor for tampering within 90 days. No need for low_signal flag.

case_studies.title: Screen Before You Serve: Simulation for Production Customer Experience AI Agents at 140M Scale
case_studies.abstract: Customer experience (CX) agents use tools and large language models to address customer requests and guide conversational interactions with an organization's products. Improving these agents, especially in regulated industries, is difficult: they must detect intent, follow complex operational policies and use tools reliably. Manual end-to-end testing offers limited coverage, while live experiments expose customers to failures that can erode trust. We present a hypothesis-driven simulation workflow for screening candidate CX agents before deployment. Synthetic customers react to agent responses
case_studies.summary: The paper introduces a simulation workflow that lets developers test AI‑driven customer support agents before they see real users. By feeding synthetic customers into the system, it checks intent detection, policy compliance, and tool use, aiming to catch failures early. The result is a safer launch with fewer live mistakes, but it does not directly change how cloud infrastructure is managed.
case_studies.it_breakdown: Not directly applicable to IT infrastructure work

case_studies.title: Where Does Exactly-Once Live? Model, Harness, and Tool-Contract Effects on Duplicate Side Effects in LLM Agents
case_studies.abstract: When a tool-using agent's write times out or returns a server error, the action may already have taken effect. Retrying blindly duplicates it -- a second charge, a second announcement, a second deployment -- while giving up skips required work. We ask where exactly-once behaviour should be enforced: in the model, in the agent harness, or in the tool contract. We introduce LIMBO, a deterministic sandbox of six services with realistic contracts (optional idempotency keys, eventually consistent and missing read paths) and twelve fault modes injected at the service boundary, including late commits
case_studies.summary: The research tackles duplicate actions caused by timeouts or server errors in tool‑using LLM agents, building LIMBO—a sandbox with realistic service contracts and fault injection to test exactly‑once behaviour. It shows where to enforce idempotency: in the model, harness, or tool contract, helping reduce double charges, announcements or deployments. This is relevant for managing cloud infrastructure that relies on LLM agents to trigger API calls.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage cloud infrastructure that triggers tool calls via LLM agents, step 1: enable idempotency keys on your APIs; step 2: configure your harness to retry only on non‑duplicate responses; step 3: monitor for late commits or missing read paths and enforce checks in the harness or model as needed.
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper uncovers non-obvious pitfalls around idempotency and fault handling in LLM‑driven tool‑using agents. It proposes a sandbox (LIMBO) that IT engineers can adopt to validate their agents against real‑world tool contracts, providing immediate practical value for testing, debugging, and improving deployment pipelines. The findings are directly applicable to SaaS tooling, MLOps, and cloud infrastructure, making it a high‑relevance, high‑novelty resource for the audience.

case_studies.title: The KV Cache Working Set: Online Capacity Planning for LLM Inference Systems
case_studies.abstract: Prefix caching is critical for efficient large language model (LLM) serving, particularly for agentic workloads that repeatedly invoke the model with a growing conversation and tool-use history. By reusing the key-value (KV) states of previously processed prefixes, prefix caching avoids redundant prefill computation. Its effectiveness, however, depends on retaining a sufficiently large set of KV cache states. Provisioning enough cache to preserve all historical KV states is prohibitively expensive and often unnecessary, whereas insufficient capacity can substantially degrade the cache hit rate
case_studies.summary: This research tackles the problem of how much KV cache space to reserve for LLM inference to keep useful prefixes without wasting memory. The authors built a model that predicts the working set size needed for prefix caching, showing that provisioning just enough cache keeps hit rates high while saving resources. This is directly relevant to cloud infra managers looking to optimise memory for LLM services.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage LLM inference workloads, use their working‑set model to calculate the minimal KV cache size you need: 1) feed your model’s prefix length and usage pattern into their estimator, 2) allocate that amount of memory in your GPU pool, 3) monitor hit rates and adjust if the model’s behaviour changes.
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper tackles KV cache capacity planning for LLM inference, a topic directly relevant to infrastructure that hosts LLM services. It offers actionable insights for sizing cache, which can improve performance and cost efficiency for cloud-based inference workloads. However, the findings are fairly specific and would require adaptation to particular deployment stacks, so the immediate build‑or‑deploy potential is moderate.

case_studies.title: FDE-Bench: Evaluating LLM Agents for Deployment Environment Configuration
case_studies.abstract: Deployment requires an agent to turn application code into a running system whose services connect, become ready, and remain observable. FDE-Bench evaluates this capability with 136 deployment-configuration tasks spanning Docker images, multi-service Compose stacks, and Kubernetes, in greenfield and diagnose-and-repair modes. Agents submit declarative artifacts that are collected, rebuilt, and redeployed in a pristine environment. Four gated binary check layers measure build, readiness, behavior, and conformance to the deployment specification, using programmatic checks without an LLM judge. A
case_studies.summary: FDE-Bench is a benchmark that tests how well large language model agents can automatically generate and deploy configuration files for Docker, Docker‑Compose and Kubernetes. The authors created 136 realistic deployment tasks and a fully automated pipeline that checks build, readiness, behaviour and specification compliance without human judgement. The result is a repeatable testbed showing which LLMs can reliably produce production‑ready infrastructure artefacts.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage cloud infrastructure, use FDE-Bench to evaluate your own automation tools: 1) run the 136 tasks against your scripts or LLMs, 2) compare the four automated check scores, 3) refine your templates or policies to close any gaps in build or readiness.
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper introduces a benchmark for LLM agents that automate deployment configuration across Docker, Compose, and Kubernetes, a directly applicable use-case for IT engineers. Novelty is moderate (25/33) due to the focus on deployment automation rather than pure research. IT relevance is high (28/33) because it addresses real-world tools (Docker, Kubernetes, CI/CD pipelines). The benchmark and example agents provide concrete, actionable steps that could be integrated or extended within 90 days, earning a value score of 30/34. The combined score well exceeds 40, so 'low_signal' is false.
